articles.body:
O concurso 3.061 da Mega-Sena pode pagar um prêmio de R$ 32 milhões para os apostadores que acertarem as seis dezenas. O sorteio ocorre às 21h desta terça-feira (22), em São Paulo.

No concurso da último domingo (20), nenhuma aposta acertou a faixa principal e o valor acumulou.

O g1 transmite todos os sorteios das Loterias Caixa, ao vivo . A transmissão começa momentos antes de cada dia de concursos, no site e no canal do g1 no YouTube .

A aposta mínima para a Mega-Sena custa R$ 6 e pode ser realizada também pela internet – saiba como fazer a sua aposta online .

Volante da Mega-Sena — Foto: Ana Marin/g1

As apostas podem ser realizadas até as 20h (horário de Brasília) em qualquer lotérica do país ou por meio do site e aplicativo Loterias Caixa, disponíveis em smartphones, computadores e outros dispositivos.

Já os bolões digitais poderão ser comprados até as 20h30, exclusivamente pelo portal Loterias Online e pelo aplicativo.

Ainda segundo a Caixa, para os sorteios realizados aos domingos as apostas simples podem ser efetuadas até as 22h de sábado por meio das unidades lotéricas, pelo Portal Loterias Caixa e do aplicativo Loterias Caixa.

A comercialização dos Bolões Caixa nos canais eletrônicos, nesse caso, acontece até às 10h45 do domingo, quinze minutos antes da realização dos sorteios.

O pagamento da aposta online pode ser realizado via PIX, cartão de crédito ou pelo internet banking, para correntistas da Caixa. É preciso ter 18 anos ou mais para participar.

A probabilidade de vencer em cada concurso varia de acordo com o número de dezenas jogadas e do tipo de aposta realizada. Para um jogo simples, com apenas seis dezenas, que custa R$ 6, a probabilidade de ganhar o prêmio milionário é de 1 em 50.063.860, segundo a Caixa.

Já para uma aposta com 20 dezenas (limite máximo), com o preço de R$ 232.560,00, a probabilidade de acertar o prêmio é de 1 em 1.292, ainda de acordo com a instituição.

articles.title: Câmara de Parnamirim amplia serviços e oportunidades para a população | G1
articles.standfirst: Mais perto de você: além de cumprir seu papel de fiscalizar, legislar e ouvir as demandas da cidade, a Câmara abre suas portas para oferecer serviços, qualificação e oportunidades.
articles.summary: Mais perto de você: além de cumprir seu papel de fiscalizar, legislar e ouvir as demandas da cidade, a Câmara abre suas portas para oferecer serviços, qualificação e oportunidades.
articles.body:
Seja para emitir um documento, participar de uma audiência pública ou buscar conhecimento e preparação para o mercado de trabalho, a população encontra na Câmara de Parnamirim um espaço de atendimento, acolhimento e cidadania. São ações que transformam a presença da Câmara no dia a dia da cidade e mostram que estar perto da população também é facilitar o acesso a serviços, promover qualificação e criar caminhos para quem busca novas oportunidades. Confira a seguir algumas ações realizadas pelo Poder Legislativo em Parnamirim.

Acesso à cidadania com emissão gratuita da Carteira de Identidade

Por meio da Sala do Cidadão, a Casa Legislativa oferece serviços que facilitam o acesso dos parnamirinenses a documentos essenciais, entre eles a emissão da Carteira de Identidade Nacional (CIN). O serviço já beneficiou milhares de moradores. Até julho de 2026, mais de 2.600 carteiras de identidade haviam sido emitidas pela Casa Legislativa.

A primeira via da identidade é gratuita. Para solicitar o documento, o cidadão realiza o agendamento pelo site oficial da instituição. Desde setembro, os novos horários são disponibilizados todas as terças-feiras, facilitando a organização do atendimento e o acesso da população ao serviço.

Para o atendimento, é necessário apresentar a certidão de nascimento ou casamento, CPF e comprovante de residência. Pessoas com deficiência devem apresentar também o laudo médico. Alguns documentos, como Cartão do SUS, Carteira de Trabalho, CNH e comprovante de tipo sanguíneo, podem ser incluídos de forma opcional.

O administrador Antônio Régis foi um dos parnamirinenses atendidos na Casa Legislativa e destaca a facilidade do serviço. “Eu agendei, vim aqui na Câmara e fiz minha nova identidade. Foi tudo muito rápido e tranquilo. Agora estou com meu documento novo e posso exercer meus direitos como cidadão com mais facilidade. É muito bom saber que a gente pode contar com um serviço assim, perto da população e que facilita tanto a nossa vida”, afirmou.

Antônio Régis fez a nova Carteira Nacional de Identidade na Sala do Cidadão da Casa Legislativa — Foto: Ascom/CMP

Mais do que emitir um documento, a Sala do Cidadão representa uma porta de acesso a direitos e serviços públicos. A Carteira de Identidade Nacional é um documento essencial para a identificação civil e para o acesso a diferentes serviços e benefícios.

Câmara de Parnamirim amplia produtividade

A Câmara Municipal de Parnamirim apresenta números que demonstram o ritmo de trabalho do Legislativo e a atuação dos 21 vereadores na fiscalização, na proposição de melhorias e na discussão das demandas da população.

Em 2025, a Casa Legislativa registrou 2.316 indicações, 423 requerimentos e 276 projetos de lei ordinária, além de 23 projetos de leis complementares e 42 projetos de resolução. Também foram contabilizadas mais de 300 moções de aplauso, moções de pesar, moções de congratulação e outras proposições. Os números representam um crescimento expressivo em relação ao ano anterior. Na comparação entre os dois anos, as indicações cresceram 12,4%, os requerimentos tiveram aumento de 197,9% e os projetos de lei ordinária cresceram 49,2%.

Casa Legislativa apresenta dados de produtividade dos 21 vereadores de Parnamirim — Foto: Ascom/CMP

O trabalho legislativo também teve continuidade em 2026. De acordo com o levantamento da Casa Legislativa, já foram contabilizados 1.157 indicações, 178 requerimentos, 162 projetos de lei ordinária, 15 projetos de leis complementares e 13 projetos de resolução. Entre as matérias que já resultaram em legislação em 2026, estão mais de 80 leis complementares, leis ordinárias, resoluções e decretos legislativos. Em 2026, também já foram realizadas 13 audiências públicas, 88 sessões ordinárias e nove sessões solenes.

Mais do que números, cada indicação, requerimento, projeto e audiência representa uma demanda que chegou à Casa Legislativa e entrou na pauta de trabalho dos vereadores. Com 21 vereadores atuando diariamente, a Câmara de Parnamirim fortalece seu papel de fiscalizar, propor, debater e acompanhar as necessidades da cidade, mantendo, em 2026, o ritmo de produção e participação nas discussões de interesse da população.

A Câmara de Parnamirim está levando qualificação e esperança para dentro dos bairros. Em parceria com o Senac, o Projeto Novos Horizontes já formou mais de 40 mulheres no curso de Cuidador de Idosos e já está com inscrições abertas para mais 40 vagas. O curso prepara as participantes para atuar no cuidado com pessoas idosas, com conhecimentos que envolvem rotina de cuidados, bem-estar, segurança, alimentação, higiene e acompanhamento das necessidades do idoso.

Mais do que aprender uma nova profissão, as alunas ganham conhecimento e confiança para buscar uma oportunidade no mercado de trabalho, empreender e aumentar a renda da família. A estudante Aldjane Nunes foi uma parnamirinenses que realizou o curso e, para ela, cada aula representou também a chance de recomeçar e construir novos caminhos.

“Ter meu certificado na mão é a realização de um sonho! Eu aprendi muito durante o curso e agora me sinto mais preparada para buscar uma oportunidade de trabalho. Muitas vezes a gente só precisa de uma oportunidade pra recomeçar, e eu agarrei essa chance com muita vontade. Pra mim, esse certificado é um novo começo”, afirmou.

Aldjane Nunes foi uma das parnamirinenses que fez o curso de Cuidador de Idosos — Foto: Ascom/CMP

Esse curso de qualificação faz parte de uma ação maior da Escola do Legislativo Prof. Eva Lúcia, que oferece cursos e capacitações para aproximar ainda mais a Câmara de Vereadores da população e ampliar o acesso ao conhecimento. Ao longo do ano, a Escola do Legislativo também promove outras formações, com cursos e oficinas voltados para qualificação profissional, empreendedorismo, educação, cidadania e desenvolvimento de novas habilidades.

articles.title: ONU defenderá sua própria sobrevivência na Assembleia Geral  | G1
articles.standfirst: Organização tem sido alvo de ataques e cortes de financiamento, principalmente pelos EUA. Assembleia Geral começa nesta terça (22). Brasil abre sessão de debates.
articles.summary: Organização tem sido alvo de ataques e cortes de financiamento, principalmente pelos EUA. Assembleia Geral começa nesta terça (22). Brasil abre sessão de debates.
articles.body:
O plenário da Assembleia Geral da Organização das Nações Unidas, em 21 de setembro de 2026. — Foto: David Dee Delgado/ Reuters

Sob constates ataques, cortes de verba e crise de credibilidade, a Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU) usará sua 81ª Assembleia Geral, que começa nesta terça-feira (22), para fazer um apelo pela sua própria sobrevivência.

A defesa institucional será a mensagem central durante a Assembleia Geral, segundo Stéphane Dujarric, porta-voz de António Guterres - secretário-geral da ONU.

"O secretário-geral quer que os Estados-membros reafirmem seu compromisso com esta organização", disse Dujarric.

🌏 Fundada em 1945, logo após o fim da Segunda Guerra Mundial, como um instrumento internacional regulador de conflitos e das relações entre os países , a Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU) é composta por 193 países — incluindo o Brasil. Há 80 anos, é a principal instituição multilateral do planeta.

➡️ Recentemente, no entanto, a ONU virou alvo de uma série de críticos , liderados pelo presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, que acusa a instituição de ser enviesada e ineficaz . Desde que Trump voltou à Casa Branca, em janeiro do ano passado, o governo dos EUA, que responde por mais de 20% do financiamento da ONU, vem cortando repasses e até programas inteiros da organização.

Países como Israel, Rússia e os próprios EUA também têm ignorado resoluções do Conselho de Segurança da ONU — para quem, em teoria, países têm de submeter pedidos para atacar outros territórios — e até mandados de prisão expedidos por órgãos judiciais da instituição.

Na segunda-feira (21), a ONU publicou um artigo intitulado "Por que a Assembleia Geral ainda tem importância?" , em que defende que líderes mundiais continuem utilizando os espaços da ONU para discutir e tentar resolver as crises e conflitos do mundo.

👉 A própria organização reconhece suas limitações atuais e fala na necessidade de reformas. Segundo o porta-voz de Guterres, o secretário-geral fará dezenas de reuniões bilaterais para pedir ajuda, mas também ouvir propostas de líderes mundiais sobre formas de manter a organização viva .

"O objetivo é termos uma ONU que, como ele tem dito, reflita o mundo de 2026, e não o de 1945", disse o porta-voz.

Em entrevista à agência de notícias Associated Press, Guterres reconheceu a paralisia de agências da organização e, principalmente, do Conselho de Segurança .

Ele culpou a "enorme divisão geopolítica" e disse que a sobrevivência da ONU depende de que os países, principalmente as grandes potências, respeitem o direito internacional .

"Muitos países dizem: 'Se as superpotências podem violar a lei, por que nós não podemos?'" Eles fazem o que querem, sabendo que haverá impunidade total", afirmou Guterres, que discursa nesta terça-feira antes do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

"A ONU deve ser uma referência de valores e princípios para todo o mundo, pois alguém precisa afirmar que a lei da força não pode prevalecer sobre a força da lei", acrescentou.

Desde o ano passado, o secretário-geral vem lutando com a crise financeira aguda da ONU, que fez a organização ter de cortar programas inteiros para sobreviver.

Para o diretor do Grupo de Assuntos Globais e Crises Internacionais da ONU, Richard Gowan, a única forma da ONU sobrevivência é "voltar ao básico" .

Em um artigo na revista "Foreing Affairs" na segunda-feira (21) intitulado "Enxuguem a ONU", Gowan defende que a organização passe a focar em funções essenciais, como a mediação de conflitos e a ajuda humanitária. E propõe que a próxima liderança da ONU, que substituirá Guterrez, abandone burocracias excessivas e cúpulas grandiosas em favor de uma diplomacia mais ágil e enxuta .

"Diante de desafios crescentes, uma iminente transição de liderança poderá determinar se a ONU conseguirá se estabilizar e talvez até recuperar parte de sua credibilidade — ou se deslizará ainda mais para a decadência", escreveu.

Em meio à crise interna, eleições e relações tensas com Donald Trump, Lula também deve usar seu discurso, que abrirá a Assembleia Geral, para defender a ONU e o multilateralismo.

O tema deve fazer parte do seu discurso nesta terça, segundo indicou o presidente em entrevista à jornalista Christiane Amanpour, da rede CNN Internacional, na segunda-feira.

"O multilateralismo é o que funcionou até agora para manter o comércio do mundo em uma certa harmonia, porque se não tivermos harmonia comercial, tudo será um caos na economia mundial", disse Lula na entrevista.

O brasileiro afirmou, também, que Donald Trump tem caminhado na contramão do multilateralismo.

"Isso é muito perigoso, porque sempre existe a possibilidade de prevalecer o mais forte, aquele que é mais forte economicamente, aquele que tem mais armas, aquele que tem mais tecnologia".

articles.title: Scientists discover why Kent meningitis outbreak was so severe
articles.summary: The bacteria responsible picked up some new genetic material, say experts.
articles.body:
Scientists say they have discovered why the bacteria responsible for the UK's worst outbreak of meningitis B in Kent earlier this year proved so dangerous.

More than 20 young people, mostly students, were infected in the March outbreak , linked to a Canterbury nightclub. All needed hospital treatment, while nine ended up in intensive care and two died.

Experts at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) and the University of Oxford, who have looked at the DNA of the bacterium , say it picked up some genetic material from other bugs found naturally in the throats of some people.

This exchange created a new strain or variant that then spread between clubbers and caused severe illness.

Experts stress the meningitis vaccine currently being offered to more than a million young people starting university protects against it.

"This investigation shows just how quickly and dramatically these bacteria can change," says Dr Charlene Rodrigues, consultant in Pathogen Genomics at UKHSA.

"The fact this outbreak variant was able to spread to so many young people was due to the social environment, a place where lots of close social mixing takes place."

Speaking exclusively to the BBC, she said bacteria are known to undergo changes like this, known as horizontal gene transfer.

Such changes can make infections more severe, and may mean they get past the immune system because people haven't encountered them before.

These events, while rare and unpredictable, could happen again, so experts "should not take their eye off the ball", she added.

Scientists say speed and severity of the Kent outbreak was very unusual . It was described as "unprecedented" and "explosive" at the time, with so many infections happening in one place and over a very short period.

Two people died - a 21-year-old University of Kent student and Juliette Kenny, a sixth-form pupil at Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School in Faversham.

The outbreak is thought to have started in a nightclub called Club Chemistry in the city centre, which was popular with university students.

It's likely one person brought the infection in with them, and then it spread that evening.

Meningitis is passed through close contact - including kissing and sharing drinks or vapes.

Dr Rodrigues suspects the very same genetic changes that made the strain so dangerous may also explain why the outbreak was short-lived and did not continue to spread.

People were generally too sick to be silent carriers who can pass it on unknowingly to others.

Following the Kent outbreak, a one-off menB vaccination programme was launched to protect young people heading to university this autumn.

In July, the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) also recommended that teenagers should be offered the jab on the NHS around the age of 15, with catch-up programmes for those who would otherwise miss out.

articles.title: New right to bereavement leave to cover step and half relatives
articles.summary: The new law will also cover foster, kinship care and adoptive relationships, as well as early pregnancy loss.
articles.body:
A new legal right to unpaid time off work after suffering a bereavement will cover step and half relatives, as well as foster, kinship care and adoptive relationships, the government has said.

From April next year, employees in Great Britain who lose a spouse, partner, parent, adult child or sibling will be entitled to up to two weeks' unpaid leave.

The government had already confirmed the new rights will also apply to parents who experience a miscarriage before 24 weeks of pregnancy.

Previously only parents who have lost a child aged under 18 or stillborn from 24 weeks had a legal right to bereavement leave.

The Employment Rights Act, which became law in December 2025, introduced a new legal right to unpaid leave for employees who have suffered a bereavement, including pregnancy loss, from the first day in a job.

'I went back after 3 days': Calls for miscarriage bereavement leave

How will the changes to workers' rights affect you?

Following a consultation, the government has now set out exactly who the new right will apply to.

It said including step, half, adoptive, foster and kinship care relationships – where family or friends take care of a child when their parents are not able to - would "bring the UK's laws into the 21st century".

Welcoming the move, the chief executive of the Kinship charity, Lucy Peake, said: "Kinship families grieve the loss of a loved one just like any other family, and this right to take time off work will help ensure they are treated fairly alongside other bereaved families."

Meanwhile, the right also covers women and their partners who experience a pregnancy loss, including miscarriage, terminations and unsuccessful IVF embryo transfers.

It will also apply to the other biological parent, or intended parents in a surrogacy arrangement.

Employees will be able to take the leave flexibly within 56 weeks of the loss, rather than as a full block.

The CBI, which represents UK businesses, said many employers already provide compassionate leave in these circumstances and it would engage with the government and unions to ensure the details work in practice.

However, the government said "there needs to be a safety net beyond this discretion".

Minister for the Future of Work, Kate Dearden, said: "No one should have to fight for time to grieve.

"These changes back people going through some of the hardest moments of life, whoever they are and wherever they work."

Miscarriage UK described the announcement as "an important step in recognising pregnancy loss as a bereavement".

Chief Executive Vicki Robinson said she hoped it would "provide a baseline for employers to go further", with the charity calling for bereavement leave to be paid.

Bereavement support charity Sue Ryder has also called for the right to paid leave, saying bereavement can have a significant financial impact.

articles.title: Morocco’s youth take Gen Z protest demands to the polls
articles.summary: Young candidates hope the election can turn youth frustration into political participation.
articles.body:
Rabat, Morocco – Nearly a year ago, environmental entrepreneur Hamza El Kharroubi was protesting in the streets. This week, the 28-year-old is campaigning for a seat in parliament.

Doing political canvassing in Tetouan, El Kharroubi says he is cautiously optimistic that more young Moroccans will win seats in parliament this year.

He founded the Environment and Sustainability Party, seeking to channel growing youth engagement into formal politics.

“The previous protests by Gen Z have sparked more youth engagement in political parties. We expect this year to have exceptional participation from youth, both in voting and campaigning,” he told Al Jazeera English.

The demonstrations came nearly a year before Wednesday’s parliamentary election.

The nationwide demonstrations began on September 27, 2025, after anger over public healthcare, education, jobs and living conditions spread beyond earlier protests in Agadir.

The unrest followed the deaths of eight women after Caesarean deliveries at a public hospital in the southern city, which became a flashpoint for wider grievances over public services.

A leaderless movement calling itself GenZ 212 mobilised largely online through platforms including Discord, TikTok and Instagram, demanding better public healthcare and education, more job opportunities, and an end to corruption and what protesters saw as misplaced public spending.

At least three people were killed during the unrest in October 2025.

The protests highlighted a challenge for Wednesday’s parliamentary election: many young people who took to the streets to demand change remain disengaged from formal politics.

More than 15.8 million people are registered to vote in the September 23 election, which will determine all 395 seats in Morocco’s House of Representatives. But only about four percent of registered voters are aged between 18 and 24, according to figures based on the electoral rolls finalised in July.

By contrast, people aged 60 and above make up more than 29 percent of the electorate, while those aged 35 to 44 account for 21 percent. In the 2021 election, turnout was just over 50 percent.

For Az-el Arab Hilmi, 32, who works with the secretariat of the Federation of the Democratic Left (FGD) in Tifelt, the lesson of the Gen Z protests is that young people are no longer willing to settle for “traditional political discourse or general promises”.

“There is a generation that wants to see tangible results in its daily life: good education, public healthcare that preserves dignity, real job opportunities and fairness in the distribution of opportunities,” Hilmi told Al Jazeera English between campaign events in Tifelt.

But Hilmi says political parties cannot wait for election campaigns to respond to those concerns.

“For me, this is the politics worth betting on: giving young people not just a place in the front rows during campaigns, but a real place in the debate, in decision-making and in taking responsibility,” he said.

Hilmi’s own involvement in politics began in 2016, when he joined the FGD after being drawn to a parliamentary campaign by Omar Balafrej, then one of the party’s prominent figures.

“What struck me was not only the campaign discourse, but the way Balafrej spoke in simple, direct language and presented himself as a politician who could be held accountable, not as someone distant from citizens,” Hilmi said.

Balafrej won a Rabat seat that year and did not run again in 2021. In October, GenZ 212, a movement with no ties to political parties, held an open discussion with him on its Discord server about democracy, political responsibility and the role of young people in political change. The group described Balafrej as a supporter of its youth movement and peaceful activism.

Moubarak Toumi, 18, who joined the Socialist Union of Popular Forces’ regional secretariat in Casablanca-Settat three years ago, sees the distance between young Moroccans and politics as partly inherited.

“A common piece of advice passed down from elders was to ‘walk close to the wall’, to keep a low profile, avoid trouble, and ensure stability in daily life,” said Toumi. That mindset persisted, he said, alongside notions such as the “200-dirham mentality”, a phrase tied to the cash sometimes handed to voters.

“Today, however, we must renew our thinking and engage more actively to build a better future,” he continued.

Toumi attributes disengagement in part to frustration over “unmet promises on healthcare, education and employment despite massive budgets”.

He sees joining political parties as one way of responding to those concerns.

Morocco’s youth unemployment remains a persistent economic problem. In 2025, the official unemployment rate was 13 percent, rising to 37.2 percent among people aged 15 to 24, according to the High Commission for Planning.

The election is also a test of what can be achieved through formal politics. Morocco’s political system gives the monarchy a central institutional role, while elected governments are responsible for public policy and legislation.

For Hilmi, that means young voters should distinguish between what political parties can promise and what they can realistically deliver.

“No party can fix every problem as soon as it reaches a council or a position of responsibility, but we can expect something essential from it: that it commits to what it said, explains to people what it can and cannot do, and practises politics responsibly and transparently,” he said.

A vote, in his view, should instead begin a relationship between citizens and their representatives, one in which young people continue to “monitor, ask, criticise and demand accountability”.

“The election is not a blank cheque,” he noted.

articles.title: Typhoon Dujuan kills two in Japan, causes travel chaos near Tokyo
articles.summary: Storm is moving northeast away from Japan’s eastern coast into the Pacific, leaving a path of destruction behind.
articles.body:
A powerful storm has triggered evacuation advisories for more than 1.6 million people, causing widespread travel chaos, flooding and landslides near Tokyo.

On Monday, Typhoon Dujuan packed wind speeds of about 144 kilometres (89 miles) per hour as it moved 130km (80 miles) south of Katsuura, near the Japanese capital, cutting power to thousands of households.

Two people have been confirmed dead, Kyodo News reported, citing local authorities.

By early Tuesday, the storm had shifted away from the coast and was heading northeast out to sea towards the Aleutian Islands, with slightly diminished winds, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said.

In areas where warnings have been issued, “there’s a risk the rain will continue as the typhoon moves north”, the JMA’s Takuya Hosomi said.

Passengers were stranded at airports after Japan Airlines cancelled 135 flights and All Nippon Airways scrapped 140 on Monday.

Some rail services were suspended, including bullet train services connecting Tokyo and Osaka, Japan Railways said.

The JMA warned on Sunday that rain and winds were expected to intensify even before the typhoon’s arrival.

“The total rainfall through Tuesday could exceed the average monthly rainfall for September, resulting in record-breaking heavy rain,” the agency said.

Social media posts showed images of flooded roads in front of Kamakura station, a popular sightseeing spot.

“There is flooding in various parts of the city, so travelling by car is dangerous,” Kamakura Mayor Takashi Matsuo said on X.

Floodwaters also inundated parts of Ichikawa, east of Tokyo.

Dujuan forced the early closure of the Tokyo Game Show, one of the world’s biggest video game trade fairs, on Monday, its final day.

A major outdoor music festival and a baseball match, both scheduled to be held in Chiba, were also cancelled.

Dujuan is Japan’s 25th typhoon this year. The country often sees strong typhoons in the late summer and early autumn.

articles.title: UK to refuel Saudi jets to help counter Houthi attacks
articles.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he has agreed to a request for ‘defensive’ air-to-air refuelling of Saudi jets.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom has agreed to provide limited military support to Saudi Arabia to help it repel attacks by Yemen’s Houthis , according to British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Speaking to reporters as he flew to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Monday, Burnham said he had agreed that the Royal Air Force would provide air-to-air refuelling of Saudi planes.

“We have received a request from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for military support, and on the advice of the defence secretary and the foreign secretary, last night I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling,” he said.

The agreement is “time-limited” and will be kept under review, he added.

Saudi Arabia had asked for support from the UK after the conflict between the Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government reignited in recent weeks.

The Houthis have launched missile and drone strikes on Saudi Arabia, including one that targeted Riyadh on Saturday before being intercepted.

They have also advanced inside Yemen, seizing the crucial port city of Mocha and key Red Sea islands, allowing them to better monitor shipping traffic through the Bab al-Mandeb , through which some 12 percent of world trade normally passes.

Burnham said he was “acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region, because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attacks, is looking at potential further disruption, and we need to keep those pathways [for oil] open”.

The UK mission will be limited to supporting Saudi aircraft defending the country from attack from drones and missiles rather than supporting strikes against the Houthis, the PA news agency reported. UK officials say the latest military agreement will start in the coming days and involve one RAF Voyager refuelling Saudi planes on “defensive” missions.

The UK and Saudi Arabia have been close military allies for decades, with London serving as one of the kingdom’s largest arms suppliers.

Earlier this year, the UK deployed its Sky Sabre air defence system to Saudi Arabia to help protect it from Iranian missile attacks during the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.

images.caption: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham gives a speech during a reception at 10 Downing Street in London on Monday [Jonathan Brady/Pool via Reuters]

articles.title: Houthis push for control of Yemen highlands as Trump is said to have called off strikes
articles.summary: By Mohammed Ghobari, Timour Azhari and Jana Choukeir RIYADH/DUBAI, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Houthi fighters pushed to seize strategic heights in Yemen on Monday t...
articles.body:
By Mohammed Ghobari, Timour Azhari and Jana Choukeir

RIYADH/DUBAI, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Houthi fighters pushed to seize strategic heights in Yemen on Monday to cut off the Red Sea coast from remaining areas held by Saudi-backed forces, after a report that US President Donald Trump had called off American strikes on the group at the last minute.

A lightning advance by the Iran-backed group this month has extended the ‌wider Middle East conflict to a new theatre and further threatened global energy supplies. The US has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to join the fight in Yemen.

The ‌New York Times reported that the Trump administration had prepared to launch airstrikes on Sunday against the Houthis after fresh pleas from the Saudi crown prince. But the newspaper said Trump called off the airstrikes at the last minute, even as troops were loading bombs onto aircraft.

Reuters could not verify ​the Times' report. The US military's Central Command referred questions to the White House. The White House did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.

Rashid al-Alimi, the Riyadh-based president of Yemen's Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, asked Trump by phone on Sunday for US military help, four sources told Reuters. Two of the people, one Yemeni and one Western, said Trump made no direct pledge of support during the call.

Riyadh was apparently struck on Saturday for the first time since the escalation began, with explosions heard and smoke visible near the airport. The Houthis said they had fired missiles at the Saudi capital; the Saudis have not commented.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday he had agreed to Saudi Arabia's request to provide defensive air-to-air refuelling for a ‌limited time, a move he described as helping to stabilise the wider region. Britain ⁠and Saudi Arabia have been close military allies for decades, with Britain serving as one of the kingdom's largest arms suppliers.

A French diplomatic source said Paris was ready to contribute to securing Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure in Yanbu on the Red Sea coast and the East-West pipeline corridor.

The Houthis, who have controlled Yemen's capital since 2014, seized the country's Red Sea ⁠coast this month in an advance that routed forces of the Saudi-backed government.

Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on the fighters' positions in the highlands, the Houthis say.

According to the United Nations, nearly 700 people have been killed and thousands injured in the fighting. Nearly 130,000 Yemenis have fled homes within Yemen, and more than 3,000 have fled by boat across the Red Sea to Africa.

Five Yemeni military sources told Reuters the Houthis were now seeking to seize strategic heights, known as the Kahboub Mountains, in two ​provinces, ​Taiz and Lahij, which separate the Red Sea coast from the government-held south.

Fighting has centred on the outskirts of the remote mountain Al-Wazi'iyah district ​in Taiz province, and Ras al-Ara along the Indian Ocean coast between the Bab el-Mandeb ‌Strait at the Red Sea's mouth and the government's base in Aden, the sources said.

"The government forces appear to remain largely in a defensive posture following the loss of the Bab el-Mandeb area, while the Houthis are seeking to maintain the momentum of their advance, despite being exposed to intensive air strikes," said Mohammed Al-Qadhi, a veteran Yemeni journalist now working as a political analyst.

"These mountains could become critical to determining whether the Houthis succeed in consolidating their recent territorial gains or whether government forces will be able to retain the positions necessary to mount a counteroffensive."

The surge in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis creates a dilemma for Trump, under pressure to help Saudi allies but anxious not to further expand the deeply unpopular war he launched alongside Israel as "Operation Epic Fury" in February against Iran.

The US bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire, and has kept out ‌of the Yemen conflict since.

The Houthis' Red Sea advance risks cutting off the main alternative route Saudi Arabia has used for oil exports ​that bypass disruption through the Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia has responded by increasing shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, where a small number of ​tankers are increasingly shuttling back and forth to bring out oil, charging record fees of as much as a ​quarter of the cargo's value to brave the wartime risk. They then transfer the oil to other ships in the Indian Ocean, bound for customers in Asia or elsewhere.

Traders say Saudi Arabia ‌has sold 60 million barrels of oil both this month and next, to be loaded ​from off Oman on the far side of Hormuz. Satellite ​data shows Saudi exports through Hormuz reaching 2.9 million barrels per day in recent days, up from just 700,000 in August.

That has helped put a cap on the global price of crude, which has retreated closer to $100 a barrel after approaching $110 last week. But consumers and industries are still paying record prices for some refined fuels, with the US retail price of diesel hitting another all-time high on Monday.

In the latest reported attack in Hormuz, ​Britain's UKMTO maritime security agency said a ship sailing into the strait had been hit ‌with a projectile, causing minor injuries to crew. It also said it had learned of an earlier strike on a gas tanker.

Diplomacy in the wider conflict has largely been stalled since a June interim ​ceasefire agreement between the US and Iran collapsed within weeks. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian is due to fly on Tuesday to New York to attend the UN General Assembly.

(Reporting by Mohammed Ghobari, Timour Azhari in ​Riyadh, Jana Choukeir in Dubai and Reuters bureauxWriting by Peter Graff; Editing by Jon Boyle, Andrew Heavens and Cynthia Osterman)

articles.title: Lithuania has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM says
articles.summary: Sinkevičius told BBC Newsnight Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Moscow, but the nation was prepared to "fight back" if attacked.
articles.body:
Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked.

Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.

He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams.

Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad.

"We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly," Sinkevičius told the BBC.

"We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us."

Sinkevičius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat".

Though the origins of the drone have not been confirmed, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it came from the direction of Belarus, Lithuania's neighbour and a key Russian ally.

The UK's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace.

"We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory."

Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine.

Residents in Lithuania's capital Vilnius were also forced to take shelter in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel.

Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into fellow Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.

Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.

Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against all members".

War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready?

articles.title: Andy Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting
articles.summary: In New York, the prime minister will also deliver a speech to the UN General Assembly expected to be focused on AI.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham said he expects to find "common ground" with Donald Trump at the pair's first face-to-face meeting on Tuesday.

The prime minister and US president are in New York City for the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.

The two men have spoken by phone twice since Burnham became prime minister in July, with Downing Street saying those calls established a "productive relationship".

"We've found a connection. So, I will go with where I feel it's right, to meet him where he is at, and search for that common ground, which I'm sure we'll find," the prime minister told reporters on his flight to the US, adding "I'm looking forward to it."

Burnham says he told Trump UK will be pragmatic about North Sea oil

Burnham says he's not embarrassed about hoax message exchange

Asked about the state of the relationship between the UK and US, the prime minister said he believes it is "as strong as it's ever been".

Burnham has travelled to New York with his wife, Marie-France Van Heel , for a day of diplomacy and a speech to the UN General Assembly, which is expected to focus on the opportunities and dangers associated with artificial intelligence (AI).

He said: "I will be making the case for closer international co-operation on AI, a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, and renewed efforts to bring an end to the conflict in the Middle East because what happens abroad impacts each and every one of us at home."

The prime minister will also announce the start of work on a new AI and Autonomy partnership between the UK and the US, focused on protecting critical national infrastructure using AI tech.

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey is expected to criticise this plan at the final day of his party's conference, saying it "doesn't come close to meeting the scale of the threat" and "only risks making us more dependent on a Trump administration in the pocket of the tech bros".

He will also call for a global pause on superintelligent AI and propose a new International AI Safety Agency.

His criticisms come after a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers.

For a new British prime minister, the first meeting with a US president has always been a pivotal encounter, but officials are well aware of the added jeopardy of a public appearance alongside the most unpredictable president in American history.

In advance of the meeting, the UK revealed that the UK and the US have, for the first time, fired an American torpedo from a British undersea drone in a military exercise.

The torpedo, described as "heavyweight" by UK officials, is "designed to sink ships and deep diving submarines", Downing Street said.

It was launched in UK waters last week from a 12-metre long undersea drone called Excalibur, made in Plymouth.

It is the first time either the UK or the US have launched a torpedo from an uncrewed underwater vessel, rather than a crewed submarine, and is seen as a breakthrough in attempts to protect vital infrastructure such as deep sea data cables.

"Our work together already shows what can be achieved when our two countries combine our expertise and innovation," the prime minister said.

Burnham was also asked by reporters about the UK government seeking to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back the joint US-UK military base on Diego Garcia.

Burnham spoke to the Mauritian prime minister, Navin Ramgoolam, on Monday.

He was asked by reporters to outline what he had told Ramgoolam, whether he supported the deal and if he had a plan to convince Trump to back it.

Burnham replied: "I said that we remain determined to secure the long-term operation of the base, which is crucial to our security and that of our allies.

"The assurance I gave was I will work towards a resolution, at the moment we don't have that, but I gave an assurance that I would commit to working towards one."

articles.title: Delhi SIR: Received an  notice? Here's what you need to do
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: More than 31.6 lakh registered voters in Delhi who have been served notices under the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) can respond online o.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: More than 31.6 lakh registered voters in Delhi who have been served notices under the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) can respond online or offline to ensure their names are not deleted from the final electoral roll.The notice tells voters why their names have been flagged and where they need to appear, while the Election Commission has provided multiple options to submit supporting documents before the deadline mentioned in the notice.The first step for voters who receive an SIR notice is to check the details carefully.The notice carries the reference number, name and EPIC number of the voter, assembly constituency, part and serial number, the reason for the notice, and the date, time and place for appearing before the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO).Voters then need to collect relevant documents and submit self-attested copies. The Election Commission has provided an indicative list of 12 categories of documents, though the list is not exhaustive.These include government or PSU employee or pensioner ID/PPO; documents issued in India before July 1, 1987 by government departments, local authorities, banks, post offices, LIC or PSUs; birth certificate; passport; matriculation or educational certificate; permanent residence certificate; forest rights certificate; SC/ST/OBC or other caste certificate; NRC document, where applicable; family register; government land or house allotment certificate; and Aadhaar, subject to the ECI's specific directions.How to respond onlineVoters can submit their documents through voters.eci.gov.in.They need to select the facility for submitting documents against the SIR notice, verify their registered mobile number through OTP/captcha, enter the notice reference number, upload the relevant documents and submit the response before the deadline mentioned in the notice. How to respond offlineVoters can also submit the required documents to their Booth Level Officer (BLO). The BLO's name and contact number are mentioned in the notice.The documents can alternatively be submitted to the Assistant Electoral Registration Officer/Electoral Registration Officer or at the designated desk of the DM office. Voters should keep proof of submission for their records. What happens if you miss the deadline?The response has to be submitted before the date mentioned in the notice. Those facing difficulty in responding can contact their BLO or use the ECINET app to seek assistance or book a call.The notice also warns that the documents submitted should support the declarations made by the voter.False declarations or forged or fabricated documents can lead to action under applicable law.Why have SIR notices been issued?The notices are being issued to unlinked electors, whose names could not be linked with the electoral roll of the last SIR, and in logical discrepancy cases, including name mismatches and unusual age differences between voters and their parents or siblings.The deadline for disposal of notices is October 29.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: 3 pose as cops, gang-rape Delhi teen inside park near Kalkaji Mandir
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A 17-year-old girl was allegedly sexually assaulted by three men at Astha Kunj Park near Kalkaji Mandir after the accused allegedly posed a.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A 17-year-old girl was allegedly sexually assaulted by three men at Astha Kunj Park near Kalkaji Mandir after the accused allegedly posed as policemen and separated her from her male friend, Delhi Police said.A PCR call regarding the alleged rape was received at around 8.45pm, following which the SHO of Amar Colony police station and staff reached the park, where the girl was found with her friend.According to the girl's statement, she and her friend had visited Kalkaji Mandir for darshan before entering Astha Kunj Park through Gate No. 7. The three men allegedly claimed to be policemen, separated the girl from her friend and took her to a secluded area.One of the accused, identified as Asif, allegedly threatened the girl with a firearm and knife before sexually assaulting her. The other two accused also allegedly sexually assaulted her, police said. The three men subsequently allegedly threatened the girl and her friend.The girl was medically examined at AIIMS, while crime and forensic teams examined the spot and collected relevant exhibits.An FIR was registered at Amar Colony police station under sections 70(2), 61(2), 115(2) and 351(3) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), along with Sections 6 and 17 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act.Accused opens fire during police interceptionDuring the investigation, several teams were formed to trace the accused. A team led by Inspector Rajender Dagar, in-charge of the Special Staff, South-East district, received information about Asif's movement near DM Office Road in Amar Colony and laid a trap, police said.When the police team intercepted him, Asif allegedly opened fire, firing three rounds at the police party. Despite being asked to surrender, he allegedly continued firing.One of the rounds hit head constable Rajesh's bulletproof jacket. Police said Rajesh fired two rounds in self-defence, one of which struck Asif in his right leg.The injured accused was taken to the AIIMS Trauma Centre for treatment. articles.title: Can DK Shivakumar go beyond Bengaluru and become a mass leader?
articles.summary: BENGALURU: The question emerging from chief minister DK Shivakumar’s pattern of touring regions, addressing local issues and holding cabinet meetings .
articles.body: BENGALURU: The question emerging from chief minister DK Shivakumar’s pattern of touring regions, addressing local issues and holding cabinet meetings across the state is whether it can help him build a pan-Karnataka presence.The strategy has gained significance in recent weeks, with Shivakumar touring north Karnataka amid drought concerns and visiting Kalaburagi for the Kalyana Karnataka Utsava.He also turned to the Western Ghats, visiting Shivamogga to seek residents’ views on the K Kasturirangan Committee report before the state informs the Centre of its final position on the issue.Govt’s first cabinet meeting in Mangaluru had a strong regional flavour. The cabinet granted Tulu the status of Karnataka’s second additional administrative language in Dakshina Kannada and Udupi, approved a special Coastal-Malnad tourism policy and cleared proposals worth Rs 32,611 crore.Shivakumar has indicated 10-12 such meetings over the next 15 months, saying every region must get attention and the govt will go where needed. Rather than waiting for regional demands to reach Bengaluru, he is taking the machinery to them. But will it make him a mass leader?Direct connection“Politics is as much about optics as organisation, and a CM who meets farmers, chairs regional cabinet meetings and announces decisions there builds a direct connection with local aspirations,” said senior Congress functionaries.In drought-hit areas, Shivakumar spoke about crop losses, water and power concerns. At the Kalaburagi Utsava, which marked Hyderabad-Karnataka liberation day, he announced a Kalyana Karnataka economy mission, a bio economy mission, a two-year anti-anaemia campaign, a 30-acre IT park and several infrastructure projects for the seven districts.The Western Ghats outreach is different: The tension is between environmental restrictions and concerns of residents over proposed ecosensitive zones. Meeting people before finalising the govt’s position puts Shivakumar in a debate with significant consequences for communities in the Malnad region.Vokkaliga identityThis could help him expand beyond Bengaluru and the Vokkaliga-dominated areas where his influence has traditionally been discussed.Whether visibility translates into statewide political capital is another question. Former minister KN Rajanna recently suggested Shivakumar’s influence alone cannot determine electoral behaviour, pointing out that JD(S) patriarch HD Deve Gowda continues to wield far more influence among the Vokkaliga community.Political strategist MB Maramkal said sustained regional engagement could help Shivakumar build a wider identity, while Vishwas Shetty, a political analyst, said taking governance outside Bengaluru may not automatically translate into electoral influence. “CM charisma and credibility, caste support, community networks, candidate strength and long-term govt performance matter more,” he said. “Whether these visits produce tangible outcomes and sustained connect for Shivakumar will be known after the 2028 assembly polls.”You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.title: Brazil election: Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro tied in latest polls
articles.summary: Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is running in October’s election for a fourth non-consecutive term as Brazil’s president.
articles.body:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro remain deadlocked in the latest polls, with the first round of Brazil’s election less than two weeks away.

Two new polls on Monday showed that the pair are statistically tied in simulated runoffs ahead of next month’s election. If no candidate wins more than 50 percent of valid votes in the October 4 first round, the two frontrunners advance to a runoff on October 25.

Lula is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term as Brazil’s president, but faces a challenge from the political right in Flavio Bolsonaro , the son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, an ally of US President Donald Trump.

The elder Bolsonaro was ruled ineligible for office after Brazil’s top electoral court found he had abused his power while in office. He was later convicted separately over a plot to overturn his 2022 election loss to Lula.

A Quaest poll released on Monday showed Bolsonaro with 42 percent of voter support in a potential runoff, versus 41 percent for Lula.

Meanwhile, a BTG Pactual/Nexus poll has Lula receiving 46 percent of voter support, compared with 45 percent for Bolsonaro in a potential runoff.

The latest polls mark a narrowing from an earlier Quaest poll on August 5, which put Lula ahead by a wider five-point margin, 44 percent to 39 percent.

Lula launched his re-election bid on August 2 at the Workers’ Party convention in Sao Paulo, casting himself as a defender of Brazilian “sovereignty” as pressure from the US administration looms over the race.

The US imposed two fresh rounds of tariffs on Brazilian products in July, which Lula denounced as an attempt to influence the elections through economic pressure.

The Brazilian leader is currently in New York, where he is preparing to address the United Nations General Assembly.

Lula met New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani for the first time on Monday. In a brief statement to reporters after the meeting, the Brazilian president said the two had talked about problems common to both Brazil and the United States, particularly the rising cost of living.

articles.title: US strikes on alleged drug boats may be ‘crimes against humanity’, UN says
articles.summary: UN expert says US forces have killed 223 people in 68 attacks in the Caribbean and the Pacific in the past year.
articles.body:
A United Nations human rights expert has concluded that US attacks on suspected drug trafficking boats in the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean violate international law and may amount to crimes against humanity.

In a report published on Monday, Ben Saul, the UN’s special rapporteur on human rights and counterterrorism, said the US has struck 68 vessels in international waters between September 2025 and August this year, killing at least 223 people.

The US has defended the strikes as acts of self-defence against “narco-terrorists”, and President Donald Trump has told Congress that the operations reflect a state of armed conflict with designated “terrorist” organisations.

The report, however, rejected that framing.

“The United States military attacks are… contrary to international law, violate the human right to life, and plausibly constitute crimes against humanity,” it said.

The findings came two days after the US military announced it had killed four people in a strike on a vessel in the Caribbean Sea. The campaign has also drawn condemnation from human rights groups, which have called the killings extrajudicial. The Pentagon has released videos of the strikes on social media but has disclosed little about who was killed or what evidence tied them to drug trafficking.

Saul’s report said the US has no right to the use of force in self-defence against alleged drug trafficking.

It argued that drug trafficking does not meet the legal threshold of an “armed attack” that would trigger a right to self-defence. It noted that international law only permits self-defence against non-state actors sent by a state, but that there “appears to be no factual basis” that some of the groups designated as “terrorists” by the US, such as Tren de Aragua, were acting as armed proxies of the Venezuelan state.

TThe report also noted that less-lethal alternatives were available, including the maritime interception of vessels – a measure that it said has been acknowledged as feasible by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Because of this, the report said the US attacks also violate the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which permits lethal force only as a last resort against an imminent threat – a standard it said was not met.

It went further, arguing that the killings meet the legal definition of murder as a crime against humanity, since they were carried out “systematically” under an organised state policy and are widespread “given the large number of victims”.

It also called on the US to investigate the killings, prosecute those responsible – including political and military leaders who ordered the strikes – and provide reparations to victims’ families.

Beyond examining the legality of the attacks, the report also questioned the effectiveness of the campaign in reducing drug trafficking to the US. It said cocaine seizures at the US border have remained steady, and noted that much of the region’s cocaine moves through container ships that are rarely inspected, and not the small boats being targeted.

It also said the strikes have done nothing to address fentanyl and opioids, which are not typically trafficked by sea from Venezuela and are the leading cause of US overdose deaths.

The report added that by killing low-level suspects, the strikes may be undermining efforts to dismantle cartel networks and prosecute their leaders. “Meanwhile, it has been estimated that the military operations had cost US$4.7 billion by mid-2026 – funds that could have instead been spent on evidence-based law enforcement, public health, and developmental interventions,” it said.

articles.title: ‘Global order under stress’: Jaishankar calls for stronger multilateralism at UNGA
articles.summary: India News: External affairs minister S Jaishankar called for stronger multilateralism to navigate rising geopolitical tensions, conflicts and global competition,.
articles.body: External affairs minister S Jaishankar called for stronger multilateralism to navigate rising geopolitical tensions, conflicts and global competition, as he co-chaired the first Partners for Multilateralism, International Law, Peace & Prosperity (P4M) Summit with European Council President Antonio Costa on Monday (local time). The summit was held on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York.Minister Jaishankar stressed the need for greater international cooperation and called for steps to address ongoing conflicts, create safeguards for emerging technologies and reduce risks linked to dominance and disruption. He also stressed the importance of international law, rules and norms.In a post on X, Jaishankar said the summit provided an opportunity to underline the importance of multilateralism at a time when international cooperation is facing pressure from intense competition, geopolitical tensions and conflicts.He highlighted the need to address the specific dimensions of ongoing conflicts, establish frameworks and safeguards for emerging capabilities, and reduce risks by diversifying against dominance and disruption. He also underlined the importance of international law, rules and norms.The EAM further called for “reformed multilateralism”, saying more participative discussions and transparent decision-making could help restore hope in the UN system and strengthen countries’ resolve to work together.Addressing the summit, Jaishankar thanked European Council President Antonio Costa for initiating the forum and said India was pleased to join as a co-sponsor. He said the global order was under stress, with a long-running rebalancing of the world taking a different shape amid intensifying competition, geopolitical tensions and conflicts.He said that if these pressures were left unchecked, they could undermine the spirit of international cooperation, making it crucial for multilateralism to assert itself more strongly."We meet at a time when the global order is under stress. For some decades, the world has witnessed a steady rebalancing, which was a long-expected structural evolution. However, extreme competition, geopolitical tensions, and actual conflicts have given this an entirely different character. If left unchecked, it would call into question the very spirit of international cooperation. That is why it is so essential that multilateralism asserts itself strongly at this juncture."Jaishankar also highlighted the range of issues that he said depended on countries' willingness to cooperate, including peace and international security, climate action and climate justice, emerging technologies, development finance, countering terrorism, strengthening supply chains, disaster resilience and pandemic preparedness."At stake here are very real issues, not just words and expressions. The future of peace and international security, of climate action and climate justice, of emerging technologies and development finance, of countering terrorism and strengthening supply chains, and of ensuring disaster resilience and preparing for pandemics. All depend on a will to cooperate."The summit also saw Jaishankar make a case for Reformed Multilateralism, with participative deliberations and transparent decision-making being highlighted as ways to provide hope and optimism to the UN system and reinforce countries' resolve to work together.Meanwhile, Slovakia backed India's bid for a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council on Monday, with foreign minister Juraj Blanár saying India, as a leading country of the Global South and an emerging power in the Indo-Pacific, should have a place at the UN's top decision-making body.Blanar's remarks came after Jaishankar participated in the first high-level Visegrád Group (V4) plus India meeting on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly in New York."We all agree, as V4 countries, that India, as part of the Global South, an upcoming superpower in the Indo-Pacific region, must be at the table as a permanent member of the UN Security Council," Blanár said.The V4 comprises Poland, Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia. The four countries held their first ministerial-level meeting with India in the new V4+India format during the UNGA high-level week.Jaishankar described the meeting as a "new historic occasion". Discussions covered political, economic, defence, technology, space, connectivity and people-to-people ties.Jaishankar is leading the Indian delegation at the 81st UN General Assembly high-level week in New York and is scheduled to address the General Debate on September 26.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: From Gen Z protests to polls: What is driving Morocco's voters
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Moroccans aged 18 to 24 make up just 4% of registered voters in Wednesday's parliamentary election, compared with more than 29% for people aged 60 and.
articles.body: Moroccans aged 18 to 24 make up just 4% of registered voters in Wednesday's parliamentary election, compared with more than 29% for people aged 60 and above, nearly a year after youth-led protests focused attention on jobs, healthcare and education. The figures contrast with the prominent role young people played in the demonstrations that spread across the country in 2025.Overall, 15,801,162 people are registered to choose all 395 members of the House of Representatives. Voters aged 35 to 44 account for 21% of the rolls, while turnout in the previous parliamentary election in 2021 was just over 50%.Protester enters parliamentary raceOne of the young Moroccans seeking a place in parliament is Hamza El Kharroubi, 28, who took part in last year's demonstrations. El Kharroubi founded the Environment and Sustainability Party and is campaigning in Tetouan, Al Jazeera reported.“The previous protests by Gen Z have sparked more youth engagement in political parties,” El Kharroubi said. His candidacy is one example of protesters and activists seeking a role inside Morocco's party system after last year's mobilisation.Yet the demonstrations have not been matched by a comparable movement of young Moroccans into parties and the electoral process. The age profile of registered voters shows how small the youngest voting group remains relative to older Moroccans.Youth jobless rate at 37.2%Economic pressures remain part of the backdrop to the election. Morocco's unemployment rate fell from 13.3% in 2024 to 13% in 2025, but unemployment among people aged 15 to 24 rose from 36.7% to 37.2%, according to the country's High Commission for Planning.Jobs were among the demands raised during the 2025 demonstrations, alongside healthcare, education and action against corruption. Protesters also questioned how public money was being allocated as Morocco pursued major infrastructure projects.Hospital deaths preceded nationwide protestsThe deaths of eight women after caesarean deliveries at a public hospital in Agadir intensified scrutiny of the state-run health system and fed wider anger over public services. Protests subsequently spread nationwide, with demonstrations beginning across Morocco on September 27, 2025.GenZ 212, the youth movement behind much of the mobilisation, had no formal affiliation with political parties. Much of its organising took place through online platforms including Discord, TikTok and Instagram, while participants pressed demands involving healthcare, education, employment and corruption.Violence later broke out during the unrest in some parts of the country. Three people were killed and more than 400 people were arrested, while GenZ 212 said it supported peaceful protest and rejected violence.Party activists seek results beyond campaignsAz-el Arab Hilmi, 32, who works with the secretariat of the Federation of the Democratic Left in Tifelt, said parties needed to engage younger Moroccans throughout the political cycle instead of concentrating on them only when elections approached. He said younger voters were increasingly assessing politics through outcomes such as the quality of schools and public hospitals, access to employment and equality of opportunity.Hilmi said younger citizens should also have a part in shaping party positions and assuming political responsibility outside campaign periods. He said parties should be explicit about what they could accomplish when in office and remain answerable for the commitments they made.Hilmi joined the Federation of the Democratic Left in 2016 after following Omar Balafrej's parliamentary campaign. Balafrej subsequently won a seat in Rabat, and GenZ 212 later invited him to a Discord discussion covering democratic participation, accountability and youth involvement in politics.Moubarak Toumi, 18, joined the Socialist Union of Popular Forces' regional secretariat in Casablanca-Settat three years ago. Toumi said frustration over unfulfilled expectations on employment, education and healthcare had discouraged young people from entering party politics, while he regarded joining a party as a route to pursue those issues from inside the political system.Powers divided between monarchy and elected governmentMorocco's 2011 Constitution divides important powers between the monarchy and elected institutions. The king appoints the head of government from the party that finishes first in elections to the House of Representatives and chairs the Council of Ministers, which deals with matters including the strategic direction of state policy.The government, meanwhile, implements its programme and the laws, while the Council of Government deliberates on public and sectoral policies, among other matters. That division of authority forms part of the context in which parties make commitments and voters assess what elected representatives can achieve.Hilmi said citizens should continue questioning representatives and following their decisions after ballots are counted rather than treating voting as the end of political participation. His argument places accountability after the election alongside the question of how many younger Moroccans take part in the vote itself.The numerical imbalance remains pronounced as Morocco goes to the polls: those aged 18 to 24 account for only 4% of registered voters, against more than 29% for people aged 60 and above. The 395 seats in the House of Representatives will therefore be decided by an electorate in which the youngest adult age group forms a relatively small share of the rolls.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Iran must stop arming Houthis in Yemen, G7 says ahead of UN General Assembly
articles.summary: The G7 also condemns "in the strongest terms" Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, saying that the escalation in fighting in Yemen jeopardises regional security.
articles.body:
Iran must "end its arming of and support" for the Houthis in Yemen, the foreign ministers of G7 nations have said in a joint statement.

The G7 also condemned "in the strongest terms" Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, adding that the recent escalation in fighting against Saudi-backed forces in Yemen represented a threat to regional and global energy security.

Thousands of refugees have fled Yemen in recent days after the Iran-backed group seized territory along the country's Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a critical shipping route for global trade.

The statement comes ahead of the annual UN General Assembly in New York, where senior Iranian officials are due to speak.

"We call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith," said the foreign ministers of the UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.

Their statement was issued following a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war

Houthis say they targeted Saudi capital with ballistic missiles

Meanwhile, at least six people were killed in Saudi strikes on the strategic Yemeni city of Mokha, the AFP news agency reported, citing Houthi-affiliated media.

Two children and a woman were among the dead, while eight others were injured in the attack on the city, which the Houthis seized from pro-government forces earlier this month .

Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised government of Yemen, has not yet commented on the reported strikes.

The UN estimates that in all, more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast.

Earlier this month, the Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen, took control of Bab al-Mandab, a narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean.

Saudi Arabia has retaliated with hundreds of air strikes in the region.

The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia, including the capital city, Riyadh.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK will provide "defensive air-to-air refuelling" support for Saudi Arabia, involving a single British aircraft, a Voyager, based out of RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus.

Burnham said the announcement followed a request from Saudi Arabia for "military support", which he agreed to on the advice of Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has also requested military support from President Donald Trump, US media reported.

Trump has wavered for weeks over whether to act on a Saudi request for help in fighting the Houthis, the New York Times reported on Monday.

The US president had earlier told Fox News that he was in "deciding mode" as he considered options for the next steps in the war against Iran.

On Sunday, US embassies across the Middle East issued new security alerts as fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed coalition in Yemen intensified.

The Houthis declare themselves to be part of the Iranian-led "axis of resistance" against Israel, the US and the wider West - along with armed group such as Hamas and Lebanon's Hezbollah movement.

Tehran has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically.

articles.title: A 6-year-old started saving empty sweet tubs; in one month, he collected 2,598 for a recycling scheme supporting a cancer charity
articles.summary: UK News: Teddy Michaelides, a seven-year-old from Netley, Hampshire, has turned a local recycling problem into a campaign involving thousands of plastic confec.
articles.body: Teddy Michaelides, a seven-year-old from Netley, Hampshire, has turned a local recycling problem into a campaign involving thousands of plastic confectionery tubs. Teddy began collecting the tubs after learning that the plastic containers used for sweets, chocolates and crackers could not be recycled through normal household collections in his area. He gathered more than 2,500 tubs over the 2024 festive period, according to the BBC, and his campaign later became part of Greene King's Tub2Pub recycling initiative. Teddy subsequently set himself a target of collecting 5,000 tubs. On 16 February 2026, the BBC reported that he had surpassed that goal, with a total of 11,233 tubs. His efforts have also earned him a British Citizen Youth Award and resulted in a recycled-plastic buddy bench being given to his school.Teddy began collecting tubs that could not go into his normal recyclingTeddy started his campaign after discovering that the confectionery tubs used during the Christmas period could not be placed in his household recycling collection. The British Citizen Award says he learned that the tubs were ending up in landfill because they could not be recycled through normal means in his local area. He began collecting the containers so they could instead be sent through the Tub2Pub recycling scheme. His family helped him gather them, while members of the local community also contributed tubs to his collection.By January 2025, the British Citizen Award said Teddy had collected more than 2,500 tubs. The BBC later described the haul as more than 2,500 tubs collected over the 2024 festive period. The campaign earned him the nickname “Sweet Tub Teddy” and attracted wider attention as his collection continued to grow.His collection became part of the Tub2Pub recycling schemeTeddy's tubs were collected through Tub2Pub, a recycling initiative run by Greene King with recycling partners including co-cre8. The scheme collects plastic confectionery tubs and processes the material into new products, including outdoor furniture. Co-cre8 says money raised through the initiative goes to Macmillan Cancer Support. The organisation has also documented Teddy's involvement specifically, describing how his collection was recycled and used to create a purple buddy bench for his school.The bench was presented to Teddy at his primary school and carries a plaque recognising his contribution to Tub2Pub, alongside Greene King, co-cre8, DCW Polymers and Macmillan Cancer Support. The project gave Teddy a physical reminder of what had happened to the plastic he had collected, turning the material from his recycling campaign into something that could be used by pupils at his school.He more than doubled his 5,000-tub targetAfter his initial collection of more than 2,500 tubs, Teddy set a new target of 5,000. His family continued gathering tubs from the local community, with the growing collection eventually taking up substantial space around their home. In December 2025, the BBC reported that tubs were being stored in areas including the family's loft, spare room and the boot of Teddy's mother's car. But the 5,000 target did not last long.On 16 February 2026, the BBC reported that Teddy had collected 11,233 tubs, more than twice his target. The total was revealed at The Fleming Arms pub in Southampton, where columns of tubs and their lids were stacked around him. Teddy said he was surprised and overjoyed when the final figure was revealed. He thanked the people who had supported his collection and said his ultimate goal was to “stop plastic pollution completely”.Teddy's campaign has received national recognitionTeddy's recycling work has also been formally recognised. In October 2025, he received a British Citizen Youth Award Medal of Honour at the Palace of Westminster. The British Citizen Award's official October 2025 Roll of Honour lists Teddy Michaelides BCyA among the recipients. The organisation describes him as a young environmental campaigner who began collecting confectionery tubs after learning they could not be recycled through normal means in his local area.The award came as Teddy's campaign was expanding beyond his own collection. The British Citizen Award said he had created additional collection points and encouraged family and friends to participate, while his efforts had also inspired people in his local community to become more conscious of recycling. His campaign has therefore grown considerably from its original purpose: finding another route for plastic confectionery tubs that could not go into his normal household recycling. By February 2026, the BBC had recorded 11,233 tubs in his collection, while his school had received a bench made from recycled material from his efforts.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
